I just downloaded Windows 10 yesterday, and I'm pretty happy with most of the changes that were made. I believe that Windows went off the rails a bit with Windows 8. I'm happy to admit that Windows 8 was bold and ambitious and made many worthwhile changes such as an app store, sandboxed apps, a notifications system, Skydrive integration and improved touchscreen support. However, it simply wasn't usable for desktop, with the user experience being one of jumping between two different windowing systems.

With Windows 10, we have the quite substantial infrastructure improvements brought in Windows 8, but we also have a sane system for operating on desktop. This system is pretty much just the old Windows 7 system, but Windows 10 also has a tablet mode which runs apps in fullscreen and is like running metro in Windows 8.

Another major feature is Cortona. I'd love to review it, except my computer doesn't have a microphone and it apparently doesn't work if your language is set to English (Australian). All indications are that it is a really cool system. One pet peeve is that you don't seem to be able to set the system to be able to search Google. Another is that I was perfectly happy to be able to access search before by hitting start and then starting to type. Since I'm going to have to type anyway, this is far easier than clicking on a box. All this search box does for me is take up valuable space on the taskbar, but I imagine that for many other users, displaying it so prominently will encourage them to make more use of the feature than if it were hidden.

The start menu is no longer fullscreen, instead live tile have been attached to a more traditional start menu. I like the live tile for weather since it allows access to useful information at a glance, but I'm not a fan of many other of the live tiles. Because of their variable nature, it is harder to find the right tile to click on than if they were static menu items. Regarding the news ones, you can generally only see one story and furthermore, these tiles are very likely to simply increase your procrastination. I can see live tiles as having significant potential given that you can just hit the start menu and then have some of this information visible, but I don't know how far people have gone in realising this potential.

Windows 10 finally provides an expose view and multiple desktops. Advanced users will love these feature, but many other users won't notice them. Windows Edge has potential to be far superior to the old Internet Explorer. It still feels unpolished, but those users who are too lazy to install Firefox or Chrome will find themselves with a better user experience. The integration of Xbox live is interesting. I suppose that if more Xbox games are brought over to Windows that that can only be a good thing.

Overall, Windows 10 is far less revolutionary than Windows 8 was. However, it made the changes that needed to be made. Windows is now truly a multi-platform system. It runs very well on tablets and PCs, we'll have to wait to find out if Window's 10 is at all suitable for phones. The implications of Windows 10 will be massive. By offering free upgrades to users, Microsoft has ensured that many holdouts on Windows 7 will upgrade. It is vitally important for Microsoft to bring users onto their universal app platform so that developers choose to target that platform. With the XBox being upgraded to run Windows 10 too, even more users will be brought onboard. I will be quite surprised if Windows 10 App Store doesn't have an extremely strong developer presence within the next few years.
